items.title: Steve Wilson interviewed by Monk Rowe, Clinton, New York, October 25, 2002
items.q: you had Rufus Reid who was head of the program at William Paterson

ctx.x: Yeah. Yeah I think fortunately, now I’ve seen the trend in the last ten years where more of the street musicians have gotten involved, musicians that are in the scene, of the scene, in addition to educators. And I think that’s been a positive. I think Bunky Green had a lot to do with that when he was president, to get a lot of the musicians involved. Of course I know that even before that there was — you had guys like Kenny Barron and Larry

Ridley who were teaching at Rutgers and then you had Rufus Reid who was head of the program at William Paterson for many years and recently retired. So there has always been that factor involved. But in the more recent times we’ve seen a big influx of that. And I hope that turns out to be a positive. Because again, education is good. But without the oral tradition, to get the unteachable nuances so to speak of the music, the spiritual elements of the music, there’s nothing like the oral tradition. There’s nothing…

Yeah. I agree. Sometimes you see in some of the magazines that you may have stopped reading, they analyze — they transcribe a solo and analyze it to death and every note has to have some function. Here’s what the player was probably thinking why he played this B flat. I’m just like well maybe he didn’t even mean to play that B flat.
